title: At the Agency Gate: The Sword Bearer Crisis, 1887
description: Translate a fast-moving crisis at the Crow Agency and compare how officials, Crow leaders, and later records described it.
learningObjectives: Describe what happened at the Crow Agency in the Sword Bearer incident of 1887.
Explain the positions of Crow leaders, the agent, and the army.
Evaluate how the incident was reported by the people involved.

player.name: Agency Interpreter
player.brief: You translate between Crow leaders, agency staff, and soldiers during the Sword Bearer crisis and its aftermath.

sharedContext.text: A horse raid has returned to Crow Agency. Agent Henry Williamson says armed young men fired into agency buildings, and he has asked Fort Custer for troops. Later accounts say tensions rose as more soldiers arrived, then fighting followed. As the agency interpreter, you cannot control every event, but your words shape what each side hears and what later becomes the record.

spans.quote:
Six of them road [rode] around
Agency firing their guns into buildings in
defiant and threatening manner without
provocation.

I called on Genl [General] Dudley
commanding Fort Custer for troops to arrest
them.
As several companies of cavalry and infantry soldiers under the command of Colonel Nathan A. M. Dudley arrived, tensions mounted.

sharedContext.text: The raiders have come back with captured horses. Williamson says shots were fired into agency buildings and has already called Fort Custer. The first task is not just to translate words, but to decide how this crisis will be described before more troops and more fear arrive.

decision.title: Shape the minutes
decision.prompt: The fighting cannot be undone, but the written record still matters. Do you emphasize order and routine, preserve both sides together, or push the prisoners’ return to the center of the story?

endings.title: The Official Line Holds
endings.summary: Your minutes lean toward Williamson’s view. The crisis reads first as defiance, disorder, and the need for firm control. Plenty Coos’s plea remains present, but it is framed as a practical request made after authority was restored.

historicalOutcome.text: The documents say the fighting ended with Crow retreat, Sword Bearer’s death, and eight prisoners sent to Fort Snelling. Later, Plenty Coos asked that those prisoners be allowed home soon.

spans.quote: In the end the Crows retreated, and Sword Bearer was killed.
Eventually, eight Crows (considered to be ringleaders) were taken prisoner and were transferred to Fort Snelling, Minnesota.

eight Crow prisoners now held at
Fort Snelling, come home to us pretty
quick

endings.divergence: This ending comes closest to Williamson’s emergency framing, though the surviving packet also preserves the later Crow council requests.
reflectionQuestions: What details make Williamson’s report sound urgent and authoritative?
How does an official report define what counts as a threat?
What is minimized when order becomes the main theme?

endings.title: A Split Record Survives
endings.summary: Your record keeps the tension visible. It preserves the agent’s language of defiance but also the Crow request to bring prisoners home and the evidence of who was punished afterward. Readers must weigh conflicting voices, not just one official story.

historicalOutcome.text: The historical documents preserve both crisis language and later appeals. Sword Bearer was killed, eight prisoners were taken, and Crow leaders later asked that the prisoners return.

spans.quote: In the end the Crows retreated, and Sword Bearer was killed.

endings.divergence: No single source in the packet presents the whole story this evenly; this ending deliberately holds separate records in tension.
reflectionQuestions: Why do historians compare different document types instead of trusting one source alone?
How does the prisoner photograph change your reading of the written reports?
Which voice seems strongest in the packet, and why?

endings.title: The Plea for Return Takes Center Stage
endings.summary: Your version foregrounds Crow losses after the fight. The prisoners, their families, and the claim that they had not done anything very bad become the heart of the record. Williamson’s emphasis on defiance is pushed to the side.

historicalOutcome.text: Historically, the prisoners were not sent straight home. The packet says they were taken to Fort Snelling after the fight, even though Crow leaders later asked for their return.

spans.quote: Eventually, eight Crows (considered to be ringleaders) were taken prisoner and were transferred to Fort Snelling, Minnesota.

endings.divergence: This ending is more sympathetic than the surviving official correspondence. It highlights the Crow petition more strongly than the preserved federal record does.
reflectionQuestions: How does Plenty Coos argue for the prisoners without denying the crisis?
What does this ending suggest about collective punishment?
What is gained and lost when a record centers community need over federal authority?

endings.title: The Meeting Moves On
endings.summary: Your minutes follow the turn away from prisoners and toward adoption, land, and routine business. The crisis remains in the background, but later readers are left to notice how quickly the subject changed and to ask why that mattered.

historicalOutcome.text: The December minutes do show a shift. After Plenty Coos mentions the prisoners, Williamson asks about adopting Mr. Cummins and his family, while the broader historical account still records the fight, Sword Bearer’s death, and the prisoners’ removal.

How should historians read silence or deflection in official minutes?
